claims.text: Selective oxidation and surface enrichment of aluminum govern the ability of high-entropy alloys to develop and retain a protective oxide layer.
High mixing entropy slows the diffusion of alloying elements.
Reduced alloying-element diffusion suppresses the formation of competing non-protective oxides.
Suppression of competing oxides fosters the growth of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale.
A continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale imparts oxidation resistance.
The baseline high-entropy alloy contains a moderate aluminum concentration and typically forms a mixed oxide scale during high-temperature exposure.
Increasing the aluminum content promotes selective formation of an Al2O3 layer.
Higher aluminum content produces an aluminum-enriched surface.
The aluminum-enriched surface preferentially oxidizes to form Al2O3.
High mixing entropy minimizes the mobility of elements other than aluminum in the high-entropy matrix.
Reduced formation of competing oxides enhances the integrity and stability of the protective alumina scale.
The increased-aluminum variant will form a more continuous Al2O3 scale than the lower-aluminum baseline.
The increased-aluminum variant will form a more adherent Al2O3 scale than the lower-aluminum baseline.
The increased-aluminum variant will exhibit slower overall oxide growth than the baseline.
The increased-aluminum variant will exhibit lower oxidation mass gain than the baseline.
Lower mass gain and slower oxide growth indicate improved oxidation resistance.
The hypothesis applies only within high-entropy-alloy composition ranges in which selective oxidation of aluminum is feasible.
The hypothesis applies under high-temperature oxidizing conditions representative of service environments.
